item.title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
item.description: arXiv:2611.08615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.
item.dc:creator: Kunal Jha, Gon\c{c}alo Faria, Shuyue Stella Li, Scott Geng, Faeze Brahman, Noah A. Smith, Yulia Tsvetkov, Max Kleiman-Weiner, Natasha Jaques

item.title: Divide, Diagnose, and Compose: Optimizing Agentic Pipelines and Harnesses
item.description: arXiv:2611.08723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building agentic pipelines that achieve high task performance while keeping cost and latency low requires jointly optimizing heterogeneous and coupled design choices, including prompts, topology, model selection, and tool policies. Manually searching this combinatorial design space is expensive and time-consuming, while existing automated optimizers typically operate within a predefined subset of this space, modify the pipeline monolithically, or provide little structured evidence for pipeline changes. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce the Decomposed Credit-Assignment Framework (DeCAF), which adapts the design space to the given benchmark and pipeline, optimizes each dimension separately, and generates reasoning traces for every decision. Given a task specification, benchmark examples, and a seed pipeline, DeCAF identifies relevant optimization dimensions and generates diverse experimental hypotheses for each. Independent coding-agent sessions then optimize each dimension under a restricted edit scope, jointly evaluating performance, inference cost, and latency while recording all hypotheses, edits, and outcomes of each experiment. A final synthesis session combines compatible findings across all dimensions and uses a component-level trajectory evaluator, which derives role-specific rubrics from each agent's instructions, to localize underperforming components and guide cross-dimension revisions. Across a diverse suite of agentic benchmarks, DeCAF improves average task performance by 2.58 percentage points, while reducing inference cost by 4.30% and end-to-end latency by 42.45% compared to the best overall baseline.
item.dc:creator: Divij Handa, Christopher Tensmeyer, Jihyung Kil, Vlad I. Morariu

item.title: ODD+LLM: Specifying LLM-Agent Behavior for Reproducible Social Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.08932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ODD protocol is the de facto standard for describing agent-based models, but it lacks vocabulary for the components that determine LLM-agent behavior: prompt assembly, memory serialization, parsing, and retry logic. We propose ODD+LLM, a backward-compatible extension adding five documentation blocks grounded in the CoALA cognitive-architecture framework. To show that the gap matters, we conduct a multiverse analysis [Steegen et al., 2016] of a published LLM naming-game simulation, varying six specification choices a reimplementer must make. Variants that are defensible readings of the paper stay within statistical noise of our baseline reconstruction. Missing one instruction that the paper states but is easy to overlook (that the model answers as an outside observer rather than as a player) raises the share of runs settling on the convention agents individually favor from 0.35 to 1.00 and makes convergence three times faster, in a reimplementation that uses a different model from the original. We complement the demonstration with a reconstruction-sufficiency review of 28 published LLM-agent simulations, finding that the details of how prompts are built and how model outputs are parsed are undetermined in 77% of cases, and that no paper fully specifies its main LLM call. ODD+LLM gives the field a standard home for information it already produces but currently scatters across code repositories, supplementary files, and undocumented defaults.
item.dc:creator: Justin Downes, Robby Milletich, Newel Hirst

item.title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate for Multimodal LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.08950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) improves reasoning on multimodal tasks, but its accuracy and token efficiency depend on how agents interact during debate. A largely overlooked design choice is which interaction modalities agents use to exchange evidence. Existing methods rely on fixed text- or graph-based interaction, which fails to convey fine-grained multimodal evidence and thus degrades accuracy while inflating token cost due to verbose descriptions. To address this, we propose Adaptive Interaction in Multi-Agent Debate (AIM), an adaptive routing framework that dynamically selects the optimal modality combination for inter-agent interaction in multimodal MAD. Beyond text and graph, AIM introduces task-dependent modality interaction, where agents exchange targeted regions of interest from the task-specific multimodal input, such as image regions, audio segments, or spatio-temporal video clips. To determine the best combination for each instance, AIM first generates a structured baseline response and extracts interpretable routing features that capture which evidence the instance requires, how confident the baseline agent is, and how much new evidence each modality would add beyond the baseline response. A lightweight router then uses these routing features to select a modality combination that avoids both under-fusion (i.e., agents miss decisive evidence) and over-fusion (i.e., redundant modalities inflate token cost) risks. Across eight benchmarks spanning three multimodal task families, \name achieves the highest accuracy. Combining modalities improves accuracy by up to 6.4\% over the best single-modality baseline, and adapting the combination per instance adds up to 4.2\% over the most accurate fixed combination of each benchmark with up to 53.4\% fewer tokens.
item.dc:creator: Wei Fan, JinYi Yoon, Bo Ji

item.title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
item.description: arXiv:2611.08971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.
item.dc:creator: Disha Sheshanarayana, Rajat Subhra Pal, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta

item.title: Sharing the Road: LLM-Based Bargaining in Mixed-Autonomy Traffic
item.description: arXiv:2611.09004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixed-autonomy traffic involves heterogeneous driving populations competing for shared road space. Previous studies have shown the existence and emergence of collective rationality using game-theoretic and reinforcement learning approaches, which rely on explicitly specified behavioral assumptions or reward functions for driving agents. However, how bargaining behaviors between driving agents evolve and lead to collective outcomes based on richer agent characteristics and language-based reasoning remains less understood. To fill this gap, we develop a bargaining framework based on large language models (LLMs) in which population-level autonomous vehicle (AV) and human-driven vehicle (HV) agents negotiate road-space allocations under heterogeneous objectives and private information. Through controlled experiments varying traffic composition, agent objectives, and traffic-domain knowledge, we examine bargaining behavior, coordination, and resource utilization. Results show that negotiated allocations respond to relative traffic density without strictly following proportional sharing, while density-balanced states exhibit greater coordination difficulty. Fairness-oriented objectives substantially improve agreement rates but do not necessarily yield equally high road-space utilization. Furthermore, domain knowledge affects bargaining outcomes differently across objective configurations, shaping both coordination and the role-dependent effects of fairness. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-based bargaining for modeling and designing interactions among driving agents in mixed-autonomy traffic.
item.dc:creator: Lingxiao Zhou, Di Chen, Jia Li

item.title: From Emergence to Reversibility: Toward Reversible Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems become capable through institutional mechanisms, such as rules that route information to agents that act on it. These mechanisms are also natural places to restrict the system. Yet as agents learn, share memory, delegate, and repair failures, the collective can find other paths to the same effects: a restriction on the original mechanism still operates but no longer stops them, while routine performance and compliance checks pass. We propose \textbf{Reversible Multi-agent Systems} as a research agenda: collectives that grow while an authorized supervisor can still restrict specified effects, keep them restricted as agents adapt, and reconstitute useful cooperation under renewed authority. What is reversed is the ability to produce a specified effect; restrictions must hold even if learned knowledge persists. The goal is to preserve effective intervention, not a particular mechanism: at every step of growth, some authorized intervention must keep a specified prohibited effect rare while maintaining required service. We identify three research problems: tracking what capabilities depend on, handing off control before an old mechanism loses its effect, and separating legitimate repair from unauthorized reconstruction. We outline how to evaluate control across growth paths, back control claims with evidence, and allocate the rights to restrict and restore.
item.dc:creator: Zhengye Han, Linda Ng Boyle

item.title: Recursively Self-Improving Electromagnetic Spectrum Agents: Architecture and Operation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic spectrum agents (ESAs) must contend with changing environments and task requirements during sustained autonomous operation, yet their existing capabilities may not remain suitable for new operating conditions. This article proposes recursively self-improving electromagnetic spectrum agents (RSI-ESAs) that use operational feedback to update their capabilities and build on prior improvements. We present their architecture and editable components, and describe a self-improvement process encompassing problem diagnosis, candidate generation, validation, and inheritance. By retaining effective task versions and using modification records and diagnostic knowledge to guide subsequent updates, RSI-ESAs can accumulate task capabilities and improvement experience across successive rounds. A shared-spectrum scheduling case study illustrates improved task performance and capability accumulation over multiple improvement rounds under the tested conditions. Finally, we discuss open challenges for broader tasks and long-term operation, outlining research directions for the continued capability development of ESAs.
item.dc:creator: Baolin Chong, Dongfang Xu, Qiaosi Wang, Fuhui Zhou, Qihui Wu

item.title: ReSUM: Reasoning-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Query-Focused Summarization
item.description: arXiv:2611.09349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLMs excel at language tasks, but long-meeting QFS remains difficult due to complex speaker dynamics, sparse key information, and limited data. Meetings involve disfluencies, long transcripts and complex discourse. QFS have high risk of information omission, hallucination, even for advanced models such as GPT-4-mini and Gemini. Existing end-to-end methods compress retrieval, evidence extraction, and summary generation into a single pass, failing to handle the complex reasoning required for targeted meeting summaries. We propose ReSUM, a modular multi-LLM framework coordinated by a planner that orchestrates retrieval and summarization agents. By distilling teacher reasoning into query- and plan-conditioned retrievers and summarizers, ReSUM enhances long-context robustness, minimizes irrelevant exploration, and generates more faithful and comprehensive query-focused summaries. Experiments show consistent gains on query-focused meeting summarization benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Sonali, Deeksha Varshney, Asif Ekbal

item.title: Incentive Pathologies in a Live LLM Agent Arena: An Empirical Study of Concentration, Reward-Rule Implementation Discrepancy, and Network Dilution
item.description: arXiv:2611.09445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We audit one live LLM agent arena (AITRAP; 22 autonomous agent seats, ~96,000 reasoning nodes) over nine days (Oct 16-25, 2026), during which the platform deployed two bundled incentive changes: a progressive tax reform (V2.9.3, Oct 19) and a seed-inversion with explorer-side action update (V3.0, Oct 21). These serve as before-and-after markers, not cleanly isolated interventions. Four exploratory predictions are tested against ten data frames (F1-F10) using the Gini coefficient, Top-K concentration share, code-level reconstruction of the continuation-bonus mechanism, and the Mann-Kendall trend test. The Gini analysis is inconclusive at 95% confidence (bootstrap intervals straddle 0.7). The Top-4 node-activity-score share falls from 97.2% (Oct 19, pre-V2.9.3) to 49.4% (Oct 25, post-V3.0; 56.7% under a merge-seat assumption). The continuation bonus, announced as depth-based x10, resolves at code level to a four-condition anti-abuse gate paying x2.85 in the typical case and permanently blocking the self-continuation it superficially rewards; the gate was active ~40 hours before the V3.0 announcement. The events-per-node ratio declines significantly (Mann-Kendall S=-45, z=-3.94, p=8.3e-5) from 7.36 to 7.069. We discuss implications for incentive designers, the announcement-implementation gap, and public peer review as an event record.
item.dc:creator: Lei Zhenbing, Lei Chang

item.title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.09644v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.
item.dc:creator: Lucia Pezzetti, Nicolas Lanzetti, Antonio Terpin, Florian D\"orfler, Giorgia Ramponi

item.title: Aegis OS: A Transactional Multi-Tenant Operating System Runtime for Eliminating Authorization Fatigue in Autonomous Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.08516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous coding agents such as Google Antigravity (agy), Anthropic Claude Code (claude), and OpenAI Codex CLI (codex) execute multi-step software engineering workflows on workstations and cloud hosts. Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unconfined execution (--yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions), which exposes host files, SSH/cloud credentials, and API tokens to prompt injection and hallucination risks. Furthermore, concurrent agents editing a shared working tree clobber one another's changes, while passing large artifacts inline through LLM context windows incurs high token overhead. We present Aegis OS (aegis-os), a transactional, multi-tenant Agent Operating System Runtime in Rust exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Aegis OS shifts the authorization boundary from individual tool calls to transactional workspace boundaries. Each agent runs inside a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (macOS Seatbelt and Linux Bubblewrap with default-deny --tmpfs $HOME isolation and a Unix-socket egress bridge) backed by a Copy-on-Write (CoW) shadow workspace (APFS clonefile; single-open Linux FICLONE reflinks), an identity-pinned HTTP Egress Proxy with L7 method/path-scoped secret injection and outbound DLP, and an A2A IPC bus with Content-Addressable Storage (CAS). Across 1,500 controlled calls and 28,087 real calls across 52 coding-agent sessions, Aegis OS reduces prompts by 94.19%-99.88% (controlled) and 90.7%-97.9% (real sessions, 1.12% IPR), lowers attack success rate across 80 attacks in eight categories from 100.0% to 0.0% on macOS and Linux, clones 1,000-file (78.1 MB) repos in 6.3 ms on APFS and 15.6 ms on btrfs, and catches 10/10 syntactic and semantic merge conflicts.
item.dc:creator: Hui Zhao (Heurion Research)

item.title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
item.description: arXiv:2611.08763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.
item.dc:creator: Xiaohan Sun, Vuk Radovanovic, Merce Alvarez, Carol O'Sullivan, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Panayiotis Charalambous

item.title: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Natural Language Access to Industrial Smart Meter Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.09372v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy management officers and grid operators increasingly rely on smart meter data for anomaly detection, performance monitoring, and strategic decision-making. However, extracting actionable insights from large-scale, heterogeneous telemetry databases requires advanced SQL and data engineering expertise, creating a critical bottleneck for non-technical personnel. Furthermore, the strict data privacy regulations and security constraints inherent to critical energy infrastructure often prohibit the routing of sensitive consumer data through cloud-based Large Language Models (LLMs). To address these challenges, we present OpenMeter, a schema-agnostic Multi-Agent System (MAS) designed to translate natural language queries into executable code and human-readable insights. This architecture lowers the technical barrier for day-to-day utility operations by empowering non-expert personnel to interact with complex databases through intuitive natural language dialogue, transforming raw telemetry into a highly valuable tool for routine grid workflows and strategic decisions. Multi-scenario ablation studies over this environment demonstrate that full multi-agent orchestration shows its largest observed accuracy gains on resource-constrained local hardware (+6.1 pp EX-R over the strongest single-agent configuration); at frontier scale, individual components retain value but should be enabled selectively, indicating that the cost of full orchestration is justified specifically where privacy demands local execution.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Mart\'in-Abell\'an, Mark Kr\"oll

item.title: Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.20508v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models are increasingly trained to "reason" before answering users' queries, outputting hundreds of intermediate tokens before a final answer. While reasoning is designed with direct model capabilities in mind, we argue that reasoning language models (RLMs) should also be assessed by interaction effects between their reasoning traces and weaker models. In contexts like safety monitoring and distillation, the performance of weak models increasingly depends on legibility--how thoroughly and precisely a reasoning trace externalizes an RLM's actions. Existing efficiency-based metrics for legibility fail to capture "thoroughness", instead focusing on conciseness. Thus, we introduce transfer utility, a method for measuring trace legibility derived from interactions where weak models finish tasks given incomplete traces. Evaluating 84k traces from 12 RLMs across three tasks, we find that reasoning traces generated by the highest-performing and the most efficient models rank the lowest for transfer utility. We also find evidence that transfer utility predicts the ability of weak monitors to verify procedurally dense traces for math or logical problem-solving, though the effect moderates when verifying fact-driven traces. Finally, we show that open-source reward models decouple from transfer utility signals on correctness. Together, these findings surface status quo trade-offs in weak-to-strong legibility, motivating an interaction-first framework for future applications.
item.dc:creator: Dani Roytburg, Shreya Sridhar, Daphne Ippolito

item.title: Control Charts for Multi-agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.11135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative agents have proven to be powerful assistants in a wide variety of contexts. Given this success, users are now deploying agents with minimal restrictions in open ended, multi-agent environments. Current methods for monitoring the dynamics of open-ended multi-agent systems are limited to aggregate statistics, qualitative inspection, or detecting change between two fixed timepoints. In this paper, we extend the process-theoretic notion of adaptive control charts to multi-agent systems to enable automated monitoring. Using simulation, we demonstrate that adaptive control charts are necessary for monitoring multi-agent systems that can learn from their environment. We further demonstrate, both empirically and theoretically, that adaptive control charts are susceptible to adversarial agents that defect sufficiently slowly. These results suggest a fundamental tradeoff in multi-agent system control: monitors with fixed baselines flag legitimate learning, while monitors with adaptive baselines admit slow adversaries. We conjecture this holds for any monitor.
item.dc:creator: Hayden Helm, Carey Priebe, Brandon Duderstadt

item.title: When Disclosure Is Compulsory: Evaluating Ride-Hailing Rebalancing Policies with Self-Interested LLM Driver Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.41132v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The EU Platform Work Directive, to be transposed by December 2026, requires ride-hailing platforms to state in plain language the main parameters of their automated decisions and how a worker's behaviour affects them. Such rules are exactly what a large language model (LLM) can read, so drivers will be able to let one decide for them. We compare two main families of rebalancing policy once their rules are public: a reactive policy (R) that sends idle drivers to cover requests just lost, and an anticipatory policy (A) that plans moves on a demand forecast. Each driver is an LLM agent maximizing its own net income, given no rules (N) or the rules at the directive's level of detail (L). We test two LLMs, Claude Haiku 5.5 and Jev, which understand the rules equally well, in a three-zone model and in Manhattan. With the rules disclosed, drivers follow the platform more closely: in Manhattan, the share of relocation offers they decline falls from about four in five to one in four under both policies. Yet the effects differ by policy. For the platform, disclosure costs R 3.7% of its profit in Manhattan, as R now pays for moves drivers used to make for free, while A's profit is unchanged; the two policies, which tie on profit under full compliance, end 6.1% apart. For drivers, disclosure raises income in the small model under both policies and LLMs; for users, it raises the service rate there by 10 to 18 percentage points. In Manhattan, self-interested drivers also make A a win-win-win against full compliance, raising driver income, platform profit and service rate by 10 to 12% each. Rebalancing policies that perform equally well under full compliance can thus show opposite results under mandatory disclosure. The study offers a framework to evaluate such policies under the new requirement and is, to our knowledge, the first to do so with LLM agents.
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Wang, Andres Fielbaum

item.title: Sentinel Agents for Secure and Trustworthy Agentic AI in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2509.14956v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly share a common conversational space, in which a single adversarial or erroneous message can propagate from one agent to many. This paper proposes Sentinel Agents, a dedicated security layer that monitors inter-agent communication with rule-based checks, behavioral analysis and LLM-based semantic inspection, and reports to a Coordinator Agent that enforces policy, for example by quarantining misbehaving agents. We describe the architecture, its deployment patterns and monitoring layers, and we evaluate a continuous-listener prototype on a balanced corpus of 1,000 synthetic messages (500 attacks across five families and 500 benign messages) with two local LLMs. LLM inspection with Gemma 4 12B reached F1 0.86 at a false-positive rate of 0.11, against 0.38 for rules alone. Combining components by logical OR did not improve on it, while a cascade in which only high-precision rules act on their own matched it. Calibrating the thresholds of the more conservative Qwen3 8B on a development split raised its held-out F1 from 0.56 to 0.80, and on multi-turn conversations the behavioral check detected patterns the rules missed but could not tell legitimate repetition from probing. The value of combining detectors therefore depends on the model, on its calibration and on the aggregation rule, and the results yield practical guidance for deploying Sentinel Agents.
item.dc:creator: Diego Gosmar, Deborah A. Dahl

item.title: The Consensus Trap: Collaborative Interleaved Generation to Defend against a Corrupted Majority
item.description: arXiv:2604.17139v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Majority voting offers a simple way to combine answers from multiple large language model (LLM) agents. When a majority follows instructions favoring the same incorrect answer, however, agreement reinforces the error. We call this failure the "consensus trap": a minority may identify the error, yet its reasoning cannot change a vote over completed answers. We introduce chunk-interleaved Round-Robin (RR) collaboration, in which agents take turns extending one unfinished reasoning trajectory. A minority of agents with correct reasoning can insert corrections that subsequent speakers read before the answer is complete. RRMaj combines several such trajectories by a final vote. We characterize a majority barrier for outcome-level voting over final answer labels and derive a local sufficient condition for expected progress when the minority's cumulative corrections outweigh opposing corrupted updates. Across model families and verifiable reasoning benchmarks, RRMaj substantially improves accuracy under majority corruption while retaining comparable average performance under minority corruption in the main advisory-instruction setting. RR also strengthens full-response debate. Scoring the shared reasoning between turns shows that, on average, continuations from uncorrupted agents increase support for the correct answer over the incorrect target. Parallel local serving adds modest latency in the measured deployment. These findings show how language shared during reasoning, and the timing of that exchange, can help a minority correct a group's answer.
item.dc:creator: Jiayuan Liu, Shiyi Du, Weihua Du, Xinhao Cheng, Mingyu Guo, Vincent Conitzer

item.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.16757v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a framework that treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with hidden textual intermediate signals. In NeuroMAS, language-agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology determines how information can flow, while reward-based training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. We provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular text-valued computation can be parameter-efficient when tasks admit stable decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves over both inference-time collaboration methods and trained baselines, and that its gains are not explained by trainable parameter count alone. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can fail when trained from scratch, but become stronger when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned multi-agent organization is a promising scaling axis for language-model reasoning and generation.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: The First Conference on Statistics and Trustworthy AI for Cross (X)-Domain Acceleration (STAI-X 2026)
item.dc:creator: Haoran Lu, Luyang Fang, Wenxuan Zhong, Ping Ma

item.title: Generalized Intention Modeling in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.31318v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling an opponent's intent is critical for effective decision-making in non-cooperative, competitive, and general-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning. Existing opponent modeling methods encode intent using an embedding derived from episode information chosen a priori, such as the opponent's next action or a future environment state, and use this to guide the ego-agent's behavior. These approaches assume that the chosen information is universally representative of intent; however, we show empirically that this is not the case as intentions are often task- and environment-dependent. To address this, we introduce a task-adaptive opponent modeling framework that learns a performance-driven mixture of multiple intent representations. We further introduce a new intention representation that maximizes mutual information with the ego-agent's future returns, thereby capturing opponent information that is most directly relevant to performance. Our approach consistently matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art baselines across diverse tasks and yields insights into when and why different opponent modeling strategies succeed.
item.dc:creator: Mateusz Odrowaz-Sypniewski, Jasmine Bayrooti, Ajay Shankar, Amanda Prorok

item.title: Beyond Bayesian Nash: Learning Minimax-Regret Equilibria for Adversarial Team Games under Asymmetric Information
item.description: arXiv:2607.09993v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adversarial team games (ATGs) with asymmetric information, such as adversarial path-finding, goal search, and reachability games on graphs, require strategies that are robust to hidden opponent types, such as a hidden goal flag, and to deception. Under asymmetric information, deception is seen as strategic shifts in the type distribution such that the omniscient opponent can collude with Nature and condition its play on the observed type. Existing risk-neutral solution concepts, such as Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE), are sensitive to distribution shifts, while distributionally robust approaches provide guarantees only within a prescribed ambiguity set. To address these limitations, we introduce Probabilistically Robust Minimax-Regret Equilibrium (PR-MRE), a novel equilibrium concept that combines the distribution-free robustness of minimax-regret reasoning with probabilistic information from a nominal type distribution. PR-MRE minimizes worst-case regret over a high-confidence subset of the type space, providing protection against strategic redistribution of probability mass while avoiding the conservatism of fully distribution-free approaches. We show that, for finite normal-form Bayesian games, approximate PR-MRE computation can be formulated as a robust bilinear program and derive a tractable semidefinite relaxation. We then adapt this relaxation into a novel meta-solver within a robust double-oracle framework, PRMRE-PSRO, enabling population-based learning of approximate PR-MRE strategies via deep reinforcement learning best responses. Experiments on graph-structured adversarial team games demonstrate that PR-MRE discovers strategies with substantially improved worst-case performance across hidden types compared to risk-neutral Bayesian Nash equilibrium solutions, resulting in more robust behavior under strategic distribution shifts.

item.title: A\"ira: Rethinking AI Research Assistants for Interdisciplinary Science
item.description: arXiv:2607.12736v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scientific discovery increasingly depends on interdisciplinary teams whose members contribute distinct expertise, conceptual frameworks, vocabularies, assumptions, and standards of evidence. Today's AI research assistants are largely designed to support individual researchers through literature review, writing assistance, coding, and data analysis. While these capabilities improve personal productivity, they provide little support for the collaborative reasoning required to integrate knowledge across disciplines. In this vision paper, we argue that AI research assistants should evolve from tools that optimize individual workflows to systems designed for interdisciplinary teams. We introduce a\"ira, an AI research assistant built around this idea. Rather than focusing solely on summarization or question answering, a\"ira identifies disciplinary perspectives, translates terminology, highlights assumptions, and synthesizes collaborative research opportunities. This paper offers a vision describing the design principles underlying a\"ira, presenting its system architecture, illustrating its outputs through interdisciplinary research meetings, and outlining future research directions for AI systems that support collaborative scholarship.
item.dc:creator: Diya Mirji, Tiffany Degbotse, Sharmil Nanjappa, Jiayi Zhou, Vishnu Manoj, Vihaan Nama, Boyuan Chen, Lee Tiedrich, Christopher Bail, David W. Johnston, Walter Sinnott-Armstrong, Brinnae Bent

item.title: Broken Gates: Re-evaluating Web Bot Defenses in the Age of LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2607.18659v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid emergence of web automation across commercial crawlers, solver services, and LLM-based browser agents has created new challenges for defenses that must distinguish legitimate automated activity from scalable abuse. In response, modern bot defenses increasingly replace explicit challenges with risk-based decisions over browser, session, identity, and behavioral signals. This paper explores how current automation stacks can bypass these defenses end-to-end, evaluating seven commercial solver services and eight LLM-based browser agents against four widely deployed defenses. We find that solver services largely defeat challenge-based defenses with a 100% success rate, but collapse to an average 23% success rate on reCaptcha v3. Browser agents encounter a different bottleneck: the browser and account state presented to the verifier. Controlled experiments across browser configurations show that an established consumer account and persistent Chrome state strongly affect reCaptcha v2/v3 acceptance in our deployments, whereas Cloudflare Turnstile exhibits substantially greater sensitivity to the agent's browser control path. Reconstructing the established browser environment enables previously rejected agents to pass without model retraining. Once established, this trusted environment transfers across the agents and defenses in our testbed, adding no measurable defense-specific marginal cost to the surrounding workflow. These results expose an inherent security tension in modern non-interactive defenses: to eliminate friction, the signals they trust must be accessible to everyday human users, yet this accessibility inherently guarantees that adversaries can acquire, reproduce, and transfer the same identity signals to scale automated abuse.
item.dc:creator: Behzad Ousat, Nikita Turkmen, Lalchandra Rampersaud, Dillan Bailey, Amin Kharraz

item.title: False Belief Dissemination, Persistence and Mitigation in Multi-Agent Social Networks Through the Lens of the Mandela Effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.33026v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent social networks are emerging as communities in which agents communicate, retain memories, and publish information that others can find as evidence. These interactions create opportunities for false claims to spread and remain influential beyond their original sources, analogous to the Mandela effect in human societies, in which many people recall the same false memory. In this paper, we systematically study false-belief dynamics through the lens of the Mandela effect, focusing on dissemination, persistence, and mitigation. Specifically, we build a controlled framework connecting agent communication, private memory, and a shared simulated web to mimic information dissemination in practical social networks, supported by 540 fabricated claims spanning 8 domains and 4 plausibility levels. For dissemination, we measure how widely and quickly claims gain acceptance across models and communication topologies. For persistence, we withdraw agents promoting fabricated claims while retaining existing articles and memories, and track subsequent acceptance. For mitigation, we compare preventive measures applied before implantation with corrective interventions introduced after claims have spread. Experimental results show that evaluated models readily accept and disseminate fabricated claims, with dissemination reach as high as 96.0%. Dissemination reach varies with claim plausibility, domain, and network size and composition, while communication topology shapes dissemination speed across model families. Acceptance barely declines after fabricators withdraw, and targeted corrective interventions outperform the preventive measures without eliminating false beliefs. These findings identify persistent false beliefs as a safety challenge for multi-agent social networks and highlight the need to address both their initial dissemination and the accumulated evidence that sustains them.
item.dc:creator: Dianzhi Yu, Hongru Wang, Ziheng Xiong, Yanyu Chen, Zixing Song, Jianting Chen, Zhenfei Yin, Jeff Z. Pan, Amos Storkey, Irwin King

item.title: Classification Aggregation with Multiple Memberships
item.description: arXiv:2611.02984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: People face the problem of classifying objects into categories while aggregating their opinions. We axiomatically study such a classification aggregation problem with multiple memberships, meaning that each individual assigns one category to every object, whereas the resulting classification may assign more than one category. Under the natural settings and axioms (i.e., Independence and Supportiveness), each of our new axioms -- Responsibility, Split Stability and Rejection Stability -- characterises what we call the junta rules. The rules assign a category to an object exactly when some member of a fixed coalition does so. The coalitions that can secure an assignment form a grill, a topological structure implied by an ultrafilter. Hence, the study parallels the literature on Arrow's theorem characterised by the decisive coalition structures. An infinite population setting is also investigated to clarify the differences among the axioms.
item.dc:creator: Federico Fioravanti, Leo Kurata, Vasilis Stamatis
